doc.title: Ray Ricker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 27, 2022

title: Reaction to Mangione with the Rochester Philharmonic and jazz degree vote
summary: Some players looked down on Mangione's project, and a faculty vote on the first jazz master's degree passed with some opposition.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: When he did his first “Friends and Love” and I think it was followed by “Together,” what was — was there an attitude discernable from the Eastman Philharmonic about this young man who is coming in with these hand-written parts and bringing in an electric bass guitar and that kind of thing? How did that fly?

Well those first two were done with the Rochester Philharmonic, which is not an Eastman thing, but it’s an organization in its own right. Okay? But right, they were older, more experienced players and you know it’s like anything you’re going to have people that raise their nose and think it’s, you know, beneath them. And then you’re going to have the other people that are in favor of it you know. And it couldn’t have been that much push-back because they were happy to take the money, okay? Happy to play the gig. And the records after that I think weren’t done with them, it was done with other studio-type situations you know. But yeah, there was a little bit but not too much. But I’ve got to say, even when the jazz department put forth the first degree, it was a master’s degree not a bachelor’s, a master’s in jazz performance. And two tracks: one in a performance and one in composition. All thought out and all the proper things that you’re supposed to do for these things. But there had to be a faculty vote on it and there were some people that voted against it but it didn’t pass you know. I mean it didn’t fail. So yeah, there were some people around that think if you play jazz it’s going to mess up your classical playing. And it doesn’t. It’s a different thing.
